project_meta.development_phase: Production (live at werewolves.hy13dev.com, played at real game nights)
frameworks_and_tools: Next.js 16.4 (Cache Components / Partial Prerendering, typed routes)
Cloudflare Workers & Durable Objects (hibernation, storage, alarms)
OpenID Connect (Authorization Code + PKCE) against my own identity provider

comprehensive_description: A free web app for playing Werewolves (Les Loups-Garous de Thiercelieux) and Mafia at real game nights, in two ways. With a game master, the app runs the game on the master's tablet or laptop: it deals the cards, calls every role in the right order with the exact lines to read aloud, tracks one-time powers and knows who wins, while players join by scanning a QR code and hold their phone to reveal their card. Fully automatic, there is no game master at all: one phone narrates out loud with speech synthesis and a live-composed soundtrack, every player acts secretly on their own phone (the wolves pick a victim together, the Seer looks at a card, the Witch chooses her potions), and the day runs a timed debate and a vote on the phones. It covers 30 roles from the base game and the Nouvelle Lune, Personnages and Le Village expansions, four themes (Werewolves, Mafia, Vampires, Spaceship) that rename every role and line of narration, and English and French. Players can sign in with my own identity provider to keep their name, photo and lifetime stats (win rate, streaks, roles played, who they win with and who eliminates them most), add friends by search or friend link, and invite friends to a room with a live invite and a push notification. It installs as a home-screen app that runs edge to edge under a translucent status bar, with toasts and sticky panels kept below it by the safe area, and a floating bottom bar that follows the phone's screen corners and blurs the page behind it when open, players can send feedback with screenshots from its menu (to a feedback form on my portfolio that emails it to me), and it is built to survive real nights: locked phones, refreshes, a game master whose battery dies, and players who leave mid-game.
engineering_highlights: Event-Sourced Game Engine: A game is its setup plus an append-only action log, and every state is rebuilt by replaying it through pure functions. Undo pops the last action and replays, so any misclick can be taken back, including an accidental end of game. Saved logs carry an engine version, and an upgrade step fills in answers that newer rules ask for, so games in progress survive rule changes.

Roles as Data: Each of the 30 roles declares its team, night turn order, limited uses and death triggers, and the night sequence is computed from the roles in play. The engine produces 36 kinds of steps, from the wolves' vote to the Stuttering Judge's second vote, and each role lives in one folder: its definition, how its steps change the game, what its phone asks, what the narrator reads without a game master, the game master's screen, and its texts in English and French, which the dictionaries gather at load time with the same keys enforced for every language. Registries typed over every step kind turn a missing piece into a compile error, as do never-checked switches and a message-handler map that must cover every message type.

Bluff Turns Against Deduction: When a role is dead, or was never dealt, its turn is still called and timed like a real one (the same lines, the same music, a random duration), so the table can never work out which roles are in play or have died from silences.

Game-Master-Free Mode as a Pure State Machine: Each engine step becomes a few beats (lines a narrator phone reads aloud, then a hold, a player's choice, a debate or a ballot). The beat machine is a pure function of the state and the clock, called by the room on every message and Durable Object alarm, which made timers, early ends once everyone has acted, and pausing testable without a network.

Per-Connection Filtered Views: The room server sends each socket its own view. The game master sees everything, while a phone only receives public information and its own secrets, so no role ever reaches another player's device. Deaths stay off the phones, the victims' own included, until the narrator has announced them, so nobody glancing at their phone on waking spoils the game master's reveal.

Resilience for Real Nights: Phones reclaim their seat with a saved token after a refresh or a locked screen. If the game master's device goes silent for 60 seconds, the room hands the game to the first dead player's phone, and the master can take it back later from the same device, or from any device by signing in. Players who leave mid-game are played by the master and dropped once the game ends, and returning players walk straight back into an open lobby.

One Device per Account: Every signed-in page keeps a socket to a Durable Object named after the account. A newer sign-in signs the older device out, and if the account still has a seat in a room on the old device, the new one is asked whether to take it over.

Accounts on My Own Identity Provider: Sign-in is OpenID Connect with PKCE against my own auth server, with rotating refresh tokens, a code-only email for sign-ins started from the app (an installed iPhone app never receives links), and short-lived signed tickets that prove an account to a room without the room ever seeing a token.

Live Friends and Invites: Invites reach a friend three ways: a live card on every open screen through their account's Durable Object, a Web Push notification (signed with VAPID in WebCrypto on the Worker, carrying no payload), and a stored record the notification reads. An invite also works as a pass: the room remembers who it invited, so they join a locked lobby in one tap for the invite's two hours, and a missed invite can be sent again after 30 seconds. Friend requests sent from the website are relayed live only after the database confirms them, so no client can fake one, and the badge and friends list update without a refresh.

Stats Without Losing Guest Games: Finished games are saved from the Worker to Postgres. Players who weren't signed in get a claim code on their phone, so a guest game joins their stats if they sign in within 30 days. When someone deletes their account on the identity provider, a daily Vercel cron asks it which of the app's accounts were deleted and removes their profile, friendships, invites, notifications and stats, keeping the games without them.

Theme Engine Decoupled from Rules: Themes are whole-word rename maps per language plus targeted overrides, applied to the dictionaries at render time. The engine never reads the theme, and tests fail if any werewolf wording leaks into another theme.

Live-Composed Soundtrack: Each night turn has its own scene, synthesised live with the Web Audio API and cross-faded into the next, with a few recordings (wolf howls, a dawn bell per theme). A bluff turn sounds exactly like a real one.

measurable_metrics.execution_latency: Every game action is a single WebSocket message to the room's Durable Object, which applies it to the in-memory engine and sends each connection its filtered view, so every screen updates in one round trip, and reconnecting sockets pick the view up again after a dropped connection.
measurable_metrics.ui_performance: Pages are prerendered shells (Next.js Cache Components) with only request-dependent parts streamed, the React Compiler handles memoization, and the floating bar, panels and card reveals animate with CSS transitions on height, transform and opacity. A press-and-hold reveal with a progress ring keeps cards hidden from neighbours. Every press answers at once: room pages are prefetched before the click (the next room code is picked ahead) and open on a skeleton while the room server wakes up, join buttons spin until the room replies, and signing in first asks the auth server for its page in the background, with a spinner in place of the account icon and a retry toast if it doesn't answer. Signing out is instant: the page shows the account signed out at once while the server ends the sign-in on the identity provider in the background, falling back to the redirect only if that fails.
measurable_metrics.operational_cost: Runs on free tiers: Vercel for the site, a 159 KB gzipped Cloudflare Worker (room server, account servers and the shared engine) whose rooms hibernate between messages and wipe themselves 24 hours after everyone leaves, and Neon serverless Postgres for accounts, friends and stats. 140 automated tests (104 for the engine) guard the rules.

star_challenges.situation: Narrating a game with many roles from memory leads to mistakes that can ruin a round: waking roles out of order, forgetting a once-per-game power, or missing that a team has already won.
star_challenges.action: Modelled every role as data and built a pure engine that computes the night order, prompts the game master with each line to read, tracks one-time powers, and checks every win condition after each step, with solo goals checked before team victories.
star_challenges.result: The game master only has to read and tap. The rules are enforced by tested code instead of memory, including edge cases like the Angel's win, mixed lovers forming their own team, and the Devoted Servant taking a dead player's card.

star_challenges.situation: Many groups have nobody willing to sit out as game master, and a shared screen can't hide anyone's actions.
star_challenges.action: Built a mode with no game master: a narrator phone reads the night aloud with speech synthesis and music, each player acts in secret on their own phone, a pure beat machine on the room server drives the timing, and bluff turns keep dead or missing roles from being deduced.
star_challenges.result: Everyone plays, including the person who created the game, and the app runs entire games on its own, from dealing the cards to announcing the winner.

star_challenges.situation: At a real game night, the game master's phone locked, the installed app lost its room, and the game was stuck with no one able to continue.
star_challenges.action: Traced it to a stale token path that created a new room and to a cleared identity, fixed both, and added an automatic handover to a dead player's phone after a minute of silence, with a way for the master to reclaim the game from the same device or any signed-in device.
star_challenges.result: A game survives the master's device going away: it carries on in someone's hand, and the master can pick it back up.

star_challenges.situation: The hosted PartyKit platform that ran the realtime rooms shut down in October 2026, taking the multiplayer backend offline.
star_challenges.action: Migrated the room server to PartyServer on my own Cloudflare account, moving to Durable Objects with hibernation, storage-backed state and alarms, and verified reconnects, filtered views, undo and persistence across Worker restarts with end-to-end socket tests.
star_challenges.result: Rooms survive refreshes and server restarts with no change for players, and the backend deploys as part of the site's build, with a separate staging environment for previews.

architectural_deep_dive.text: The frontend is a Next.js 16 app on Vercel using Cache Components (Partial Prerendering) and the React Compiler, served per language under /en and /fr, with rules, roles and FAQ guides for search engines, and installable as a PWA. All rules live in a framework-free TypeScript engine shared by the server and the client. The realtime backend is a Cloudflare Worker built with PartyServer and two kinds of Durable Objects: one per room, which stores the setup and action log, replays them into the current state, runs the game-master-free mode on alarms, and sends each connection a filtered view; and one per account, which every signed-in page connects to for single-device sign-in, live invites and friend requests. Accounts come from my own OpenID Connect provider: the Next.js server keeps the tokens in cookies and mints short-lived signed tickets that the Durable Objects verify. Stats, friends, invites and push subscriptions live in Neon Postgres: the Worker saves each finished game and records invites, and Next.js route handlers serve stats and manage friends. Themes and translations are applied only in the UI layer, so the same engine powers every theme and language.

lessons_learned: Event sourcing paid off again and again: once state is a pure replay of actions, undo, persistence, server restarts and even rule changes in the middle of a game come almost for free, and the engine can be tested without a UI or a network. The same idea carried the game-master-free mode, written as a pure function of state and time. Real game nights were the best test suite: a locked phone, an installed app that never refreshes, or a player who walks out mid-game exposed problems no unit test would have found, and each fix made the app sturdier. Finally, depending on a hosted realtime platform is a risk worth planning for, and keeping the server thin made the move to self-hosted Durable Objects quick.
